candidates.source_title: ‘Pupils are proud of their school and enjoy learning’, says Ofsted - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Ofsted inspectors have highlighted the personal development and wellbeing of students, as well as attendance and behaviour at Cardinal Langley RC High School. The Middleton high school also met the expected standards for achievement, curriculum and teaching, inclusion, leadership and governance and post-16 provision as inspectors recognised that “pupils are proud of their school . . . and enjoy their learning”. The report by lead inspector Richard Wakefield, follows the inspectors’ visit on June 9 and returning 9 July 9. Receiving a strong standard for attendance and behaviour, the inspectors said: “Pupils’ overall attendance, including disadvantaged pupils and those with special educational needs and/or disabilities, has consistently improved and is significantly above the national average. “Leaders create a calm and caring environment where positive behaviour is expected. Pupils are polite and respectful in lessons and at social times. “They cooperate well with each other and build supportive relationships with staff. Pupils are not allowed to use mobile phones in school and have begun to develop other interests together, such as playing board games. This is developing their communication skills. Year 12 students visit Lancaster University as part of their Next Steps week. Image: Cardinal Langley “Leaders monitor unwanted behaviours, such as bullying. Pupils know that these behaviours are not tolerated. Staff deal quickly and effectively with any issues that do arise. Leaders provide proactive support for a small minority of pupils who need help to improve their behaviour.”

candidates.source_title: Gareth Ainsworth sees a bit of John Barnes in James Brophy’s goal at Rochdale - hampshirechronicle.co.uk
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Gillingham boss Gareth Ainsworth hailed two-goal James Brophy’s brilliance following the 4-1 victory against 10-man Rochdale at the Crown Oil Arena. Brophy opened the scoring with an impressive curling shot in the 32nd minute, but it was his 68th-minute second, and Gillingham’s fourth, that had Ainsworth purring. “The way we are passing the ball around is much better than we have done under me and the goals were brilliant, especially James Brophy’s second,” he said. “Everyone’s going to be talking about that. His first goal wasn’t bad but the second was the goal of the season! If anyone remembers John Barnes scoring against Brazil at the Maracana in 1984, James Brophy did it at Spotland in 2026! “His team-mates made a couple of good runs to split their defence, in fairness, but it was a quality goal. He has epitomised us this season, he’s a positive character, never stops working. “This was a great performance away from home, yes we had a 10-man situation halfway through the second half, but we looked like the aggressive team from the off, the team that was going to score. And I believe we can be ever better. “I’ve been waiting for that performance and result after I’d been reminded that we hadn’t won in four, even if we were three unbeaten!” In between Brophy’s two goals, Gillingham had netted twice in the space of three minutes early in the second half to take the Sky Bet League Two game away from Rochdale. Omar Beckles scored the second on 53 minutes after Dale failed to clear a corner before Lamin Sillah headed home the third.

Despite losing both Zech Obiero, who was carried off on a stretcher, and Will Goodwin early on, the visitors took the lead in the 32nd minute when James Brophy curled a shot wide of Nils Ramming. Omar Beckles doubled the lead in the 53rd minute, pouncing on a loose ball six yards from goal – and the home side capitulated thereafter. Three minutes later Lamin Sillah effectively wrapped up the three points. Eli King’s delivery was nodded down by Andy Smith and Sillah headed home. Dale were reduced to 10 men when Ed Francis saw red for a second bookable offence on the hour mark. Gills stopper Oliver Wright made a fine double save to deny Mani Dieseruvwe and Luke Hannant before Brophy scored a superb fourth. Midway through the second half Brophy drifted in from the left and dribbled the ball round four defenders before beating Ramming from close range. Dale debutant Charlie Tasker headed an 87th minute reply for the home side.

The café, on the ground floor of the 19th century manor house in Rochdale, is being run by local Community Interest Company Get Together After Serving (GTAS). Staffed entirely by former armed forces personnel and their families, the café has been welcoming visitors all week ahead of the official opening today. Set up by Rochdale residents Adam Trennery, Wayne Traynor and Wayne Simms, GTAS aims to support the local veteran community in a number of ways, including through wellbeing programmes and local events and get-togethers. Customers can expect café favourites like hot and cold sandwiches, cakes, breakfasts and tea and coffee. candidates.source_title: 'Something dangerous' fed to Rochdale horse by campers, owner says - ManchesterWorld
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A horrified horse owner found her beloved pet trembling helplessly on the ground and close to death after he was fed dangerous scraps by campers. Julie Kershaw, 58, raced to the field where she keeps 13-year-old Frank to find him shaking uncontrollably, barely able to walk and battling a potentially fatal infection. As he lay stricken on the grass in Rochdale, Gtr Manchester., the terrified owner feared Frank would not survive the night - as she said she believes campers fed him human food. Julie said: "With the state he was in, I didn't think he was going to be alive in the morning. "He was really shaking and couldn't walk." Julie does not know exactly what Frank ate, but is convinced he was fed something dangerous by visitors because he has lived safely in the same field throughout his life. Frank had been discovered in distress by 13-year-old Freya and her mum Rachel while they were out walking. They saw the horse suddenly collapse, roll onto his side and begin breathing heavily as his whole body shook. Freya remained beside him and offered comfort while Rachel issued a frantic Facebook appeal to find his owner. Julie had been out all day when her daughter, who was on the phone to a friend, alerted her to the drama. The bistro worker, who lives around 15 minutes away from the field, immediately realised the stricken animal was Frank. She said: "I must have had 20 phone calls and it was all over Facebook." Julie and others managed to get Frank into a stable before a vet arrived within 40 minutes. He needed four injections during an emergency visit which continued until around 10.30pm. Julie said: "They told us it was colitis and said it was an infection in the colon. He was in a critical condition. "It's just so scary - people don't realise how dangerous it is to feed horses." Julie was warned the inflammation could spread and prove fatal. Horse owners have previously discovered chicken bones, tomatoes, red onions and lemons dumped among the animals. In one incident, Julie said she spent weeks picking Brussels sprouts out of the field last Christmas when visitors threw them for horses. She said: "It keeps happening and it’s a nightmare. A horse is part of a family, so I was so upset and stressed. "The vet bill was £235, but we also had to spend on food - I spent about £300 in altogether. "It all happened because of people's ignorance. "Everyone has a phone - so why can't they just search what you can and can't feed a horse?" Julie said the situation has worsened since walkers discovered the previously quiet spot during the pandemic. Fellow horse owner Patsy said visitors had even been spotted standing beside the animals carrying a chicken kebab and naan bread. Julie warned that even conventional treats such as apples and carrots can become dangerous if dozens of visitors each feed them to the horses.

candidates.source_title: Avoidable Deaths Rise in Rochdale as Alcohol, Drugs, Smoking Bite - streamlinefeed.co.ke
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale's avoidable deaths are rising as alcohol, drugs and smoking drive harm above national averages; a new council report sets out the response. Rochdale built the co-operative movement and much of the modern welfare argument; today the borough's hardest statistic is that more of its residents are dying from causes that treatment, prevention or a little more money could have avoided. A Tackling Addiction report presented to the town hall this week identifies the three drivers as alcohol, drugs and smoking, and concedes that avoidable deaths are rising even where consumption is not. The National Drug Treatment Monitoring System estimates that 2,905 people in Rochdale are dependent on alcohol and 1,831 use opiates or crack cocaine. Alcohol-related deaths run well above the national average, with a sharp spike in 2020 around the pandemic. Smoking tells the same story in slower motion. The rate has fallen but stands at 12.7%, against a national average of 10.9%, which equates to roughly 22,000 adult smokers. The report estimates Rochdale residents spend £66.2 million (about KES 11.6 billion) a year on tobacco, legal and illegal, and hospital admissions linked to smoking run above average. The report finds no evidence that more people are drinking, but the harm caused is increasing, and it attributes the gap to long-term heavy drinking behaviours laid down a decade or more ago. Kuiama Thompson, Rochdale's Director of Public Health and Communities, told councillors that drug and alcohol harm continues to have a significant impact on the borough. The wider data agree. Rochdale records the lowest healthy life expectancy in Greater Manchester, about 54.2 years for men and 58 for women, and the borough's mortality JSNA shows premature death tracking deprivation ward by ward. Measures in the report also extend to vaping and gambling, which officials now treat as part of the same addiction system. The report's language is notably unsentimental: alcohol is woven into life across the borough, and when something becomes that normalised the harm it causes becomes harder to see.

For treatment for drug and alcohol issues, increased outreach work and follow ups as well as working with different groups of people such as the homeless, women and over 50s. The annual canvass is used to check that information held on the electoral register for each address remains accurate and up to date.

Police temporarily closed the road while dealing with the vehicles.

Chief Inspector Kabal thanked members of the public who reported the driving and asked anyone with footage of the incident, including dashcam or CCTV recordings, to contact GMP.

candidates.source_title: Veterans to run new café in restored Rochdale manor house - Roch Valley Radio
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
The ground floor of Denehurst House in Denehurst Park will be run by a local organisation supporting former armed forces personnel.

The café will be managed by Community Interest Company Get Together After Serving, known as GTAS, and staffed by veterans and members of their families.

GTAS was set up by Rochdale residents Adam Trennery, Wayne Traynor and Wayne Simms and provides support for veterans through wellbeing programmes, events and get-togethers.

The café will serve hot and cold sandwiches, cakes, breakfasts, tea and coffee. The organisation also plans to work with other local businesses to offer Friday specials.

Rochdale Borough Council owns Denehurst House and commissioned local builders H Bell and Sons and interior design specialists to renovate the building.

Period features including its ornate coving and bay windows have been retained.

The council is considering using the remainder of Denehurst House as accommodation for local veterans and has completed a public consultation on the proposal.

Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for housing and regeneration, said: “This has been a really important project for us and it’s great to see it coming to fruition.

“Not only was this a derelict old building, which has been lovingly brought back to life, but it will be run by local veterans and their loved ones.”

Adam Trennery, a director of GTAS and local veteran, said: “We’re made up to have the opportunity to open a café in this brilliant space. It means a lot to me personally, as I live round the corner and I’ve always thought having a café in that lovely park would be great.

“We’re really excited that we can use this as a base to further our support for veterans, while also welcoming the wider community.”

Denehurst House was built for Alderman Robert Turner, founder of Turner Brothers Asbestos company, in the 1890s.

The house and its grounds were donated to the town in 1932 and the building was later used as council offices before becoming empty.

The café formally opens on Saturday, September 5.

It will open every day from 9am until 6pm between May and October and from 9am until 4pm between November and April.

candidates.source_title: Big problem remains: The big talking points from Shrewsbury Town’s Rochdale defeat - shropshirestar.com
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Losing football matches will happen. It was always going to happen for Shrewsbury Town. But this was a second very poor showing in the space of seven days. Managers sometimes talk about there being a ‘way to lose a game’. This was not it. Just like at Fleetwood Town seven days earlier, Salop were dismantled and there was never really a feeling they were going to find a way back into the game. Here are some talking points from Town’s miserable night at Rochdale. Boss Gavin Cowan stuck with his winning side, making just one change to the bench as Kian McMahon-Brown came in. But Town could not replicate the performance that had earned victory over Salford City. As Cowan admitted afterwards, several individuals were simply missing on the night and well below the level required. Town had been resilient and resolute to claim a first clean sheet of the season against Salford. That defensive solidity disappeared again at Rochdale. Salop have now conceded 12 goals in their opening five games, while scoring just three. And that brings us back to the biggest problem they struggled with last season: goals. So far, the summer recruits have done little to suggest that issue has been solved. The midfield was passive as Luca Hoole was isolated and beaten for the cross that led to Rochdale’s opener, while Josh Ruffels’ mis-clearance presented the hosts with their second. Sound familiar? It was only seven days earlier that Town had been punished for similar mistakes at Fleetwood. For the final blow, Town were dispossessed far too easily and Rochdale broke quickly, with Will Brook staying rooted to the edge of his six-yard box as the goal gaped. Captain Will Boyle had been Town’s hero against Salford. He can take some credit for his efforts again, but there was little he could do to rescue his side this time around - making it a disappointing night for the birthday boy. Shrewsbury have now failed to score in each of their last four away league games. They last endured a longer run without scoring on the road in November 2023 - when they also went four games without finding the net. Town altered their shape several times throughout the game. They started with a back four rather than the back five used previously and moved into a 4-4-1-1 towards the end of the first half. They appeared to switch again to a 4-2-3-1 after the break as Cowan looked for a way back into the game. Kian McMahon-Brown made his Town debut just a day after joining on a season-long loan from Burnley. He replaced Isaac Fletcher, who struggled to make a significant impact. Town will hope McMahon-Brown can provide some of the spark going forward that has been missing, with supporters hoping he can have a similar impact to Iwan Morgan’s loan spell last season. There was also a first glimpse of Michael Golding, who replaced Tom Sang. The Leicester City loanee went close late on, with his low effort being blocked. Just as they did after the defeat at Fleetwood, Town have now set themselves the task of responding to another miserable night. They have little time to dwell on it, with a trip to Fleetwood next up and a chance to produce a very different outcome to their EFL Cup thrashing there.

candidates.source_title: Ian Watson lauds Rochdale’s ‘courage and bravery’ in win over Shrewsbury - cumnockchronicle.com
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale produced the kind of performance boss Ian Watson has been waiting for as they swept Shrewsbury aside with a 3-0 victory at the Crown Oil Arena. Baba Adeeko fired them ahead in the 33rd minute before Luke Hannant lofted a beautiful finish over Shrews stopper Will Brook 10 minutes later. Dale goalkeeper Nils Ramming pulled off a fine save after the break to keep out Will Boyle’s header, but the home side’s lead was never under threat and they rounded off a fine display with substitute Jonny Smith firing into the roof of the net in the 80th minute. It was the club’s first win since returning to the EFL and the first three-point return of Watson’s tenure. He said: “I never get obsessed with the scoreboard, it’s been performances that have not looked as we wanted them to look, so it was the way we played, the courage and bravery we showed, that was the most pleasing thing. “We needed to get that first win over the line. We’d spoken about not being anxious and not playing the scoreboard but playing how we want to play and enjoying being out there. “You could see we were playing without fear. The boys want to win so much and run so hard that it can sometimes manifest as anxiety. We’ve been playing with a little bit of fear, being shy with the ball. “That’s been the hard thing for me as a coach, you want it to look a certain way and it hasn’t been that – tonight it was that. Now we have to make sure that is us every week.”

candidates.source_title: Once bustling, the Seven Sisters in Rochdale is now a very different story - Manchester Evening News
candidates.source_body_excerpt: More than 600 homes now sit empty in Rochdale almost one year on from a decision to evict the remaining 228 households from the Seven Sisters. Now only 100 households are left waiting to find a new home out of around 760 total flats. In October 2025 Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) announced they would be emptying all the homes in the iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks , which is actually named College Bank. This came as a shock to many residents still living there, with some initially fearing they’d need to be out before Christmas . Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter Landlord RBH later clarified these evictions would take place over the course of 18 months. Just over 10 months later, 117 households have accepted new accommodation. More have left through what RBH called ‘natural attrition’, which means they left through other reasons than eviction such as tenancies ending, moved out of their own accord or death in some cases. This leaves just over half of the original residents in need of rehousing. RBH explained a number of safety issues flagged in a recent building survey meant everyone needed to move out. Structural and electrical issues; problems with the water pumping system; roof damage; and the ever-increasing costs for customers to heat and light their homes were all raised in the surveys. At the time of the eviction announcement, RBH said all tenants will be supported to move over the coming months, with financial support offered by the social housing landlord. Leaseholders who own their own homes would have their flats bought at market value, according to RBH. An update from RBH read: “At College Bank, we continue to support our customers to move into their new homes. As of 26 August, 117 households at College Bank have now accepted offers to move, 82 of whom have already moved with a further 35 making final preparations to do so. “This means that the number of households remaining to rehouse is now under 100.” This update is the latest in a long saga lasting almost a decade. In 2017, RBH revealed plans to demolish four of the high-rises and redevelop them. This sparked local backlash, with local campaigners from the Save the Seven Sisters (ST7S) group fighting to stop the plans. Although demolition was eventually ruled out in 2023, a twist in the tale came last October when RBH put ‘all options back on the table’. After coming out of an ‘exclusivity agreement’ with Legal and General, which looked into a cost-effective way to refurbish Mitchell Hey, Dunkirk Rise, Tentercroft and Town Mill Brow tower blocks, the social housing operator refused to rule out razing them to the ground. Still, RBH says no decision on the potential demolition of the tower blocks has been made. Mark Slater, chair of ST7S, said at the time of the eviction announcement: “This certainly feels like a step back. But as a campaign group we’ll do what we’ve always done, and that is regroup. “I don’t accept that we all have to move out. It’s not a reality I am considering. “RBH, overnight have made a decision to inform tenants that there are some safety issues. No matter how they qualify it by saying they’re not immediate, they’ve now put the fox in the hen house because people will panic. “At the moment they are mounting a campaign of social vandalism. It’s demolition by the back door. “Suggesting the blocks need to be clear ‘before they make a decision’, that would suggest the decision has already been made

candidates.source_title: BFA joins forces with Didac and ROHS for Health and Safety Day - Big Furniture Group
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The British Furniture Association (BFA) has partnered with Didac to deliver a hands-on health and safety seminar, hosted by Rochdale Occupational Health. Bringing together expert-led presentations, live face-fit testing and legislative updates, the Behind the Mask seminar is tailored to specific risks faced by workers in the furniture industry. Ideal for business owners and directors in furniture manufacturing the session is also aimed at health and safety managers, HR managers with responsibility for workforce health and safety and anyone responsible for PPE provision or COSHH compliance. BFA MD Phil Spademan said: “By partnering with Didac and ROHS, the BFA can provide its members with carefully curated health and safety training that is meaningful and relevant. “Behind the Mask offers a combination of practical hands-on experience that is applicable in the workplace, with expert insight and technical detail that supports legislative compliance.” The seminar will include workshops on hearing, respiratory risks, failure to fit and stress in the workplace, along with a session with PPE specialists JSP. Open to BFA members and clients of ROHS, the Behind the Mask Health and Safety Day takes place at ROHS in Rochdale on Wednesday 30 th September. Helen Yates, General Manager at ROHS, said: “Events like Behind the Mask matter because they put people first. “It’s not just about ticking a legislative box it’s about giving employers the confidence and the practical tools to protect their workforce properly.
